_about: Graded text markers. 'patterns' are matched one by one by scan_artifacts.py and every hit is quoted. 'style' lexicons are counted per 1,000 words by stylometry.py and compared with the human calibration distribution; they are never evidence on their own. Tiers: conclusive (one hit settles that an AI tool's output was pasted in, once Claude confirms in context it is not a quotation or a discussion of AI), strong, moderate, weak. 'shows' says what a hit proves, which is not always 'AI wrote this'. Every pattern has positive and negative examples that selftest.py checks. Edit through the Learn step; record_feedback.py logs every change.

patterns.shows: Text was copied from a ChatGPT answer: this is one of its internal citation tokens, which nobody types.
A link was copied from a chatbot answer (ChatGPT, Copilot, Grok, Perplexity). Proves a chatbot was used to find sources, not that it wrote the text.
Interface text from a chatbot window (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot) was pasted together with the answer.

patterns.shows: Chat-interface Markdown (bold markers, '#' headings, '---' rules, code fences) survives in a PDF or Word document, where nobody types it. Typical of text pasted from a chatbot.
Text was copied from Google Gemini (often Deep Research or Canvas): these citation markers are left in when its answers are pasted.
Text was copied from xAI's Grok: these are its unrendered citation components.
Raw output of a reasoning model or a chat template was pasted: thinking tags or special tokens (DeepSeek-R1, Qwen and similar).
A reasoning model's status line or the first words of its hidden reasoning were pasted ('Thought for 12 seconds', 'Okay, so the user wants').

pos: Okay, so the user wants a summary of
neg: we thought for a long time

patterns.shows: Chat transcript labels for the assistant's turn left at the start of a line.

Invisible characters (zero-width spaces or joiners, word joiners, byte-order marks) inside running text. They are typed by nobody and are typical of text copied from chat interfaces; some converters also insert them.
Narrow no-break spaces (U+202F), reported in 2025 in output of OpenAI's o3/o4-mini models. Also normal in French and SI typesetting, so it counts only as context.
Phrases that assistants use when answering a request about a text ('based on the text', 'according to the provided text', 'I aim to'). Odd in a document written from scratch.
patterns.regex: \b(?:based on|according to) the (?:provided |given |above )?(?:text|document|information provided|passage)\b|\bI aim to\b|\bin the (?:provided|given) (?:text|document|context)\b|\b(?:the|this) (?:provided|given) (?:manuscript|paper|text) (?:presents|describes)\b

pos: Based on the provided text, the authors propose
I aim to provide a balanced assessment

patterns.shows: A paraphrasing tool replaced established terms with synonyms ('profound learning' for 'deep learning'). Points to a paraphraser or a paper mill, not an LLM; publishers treat it as misconduct.

pos: we applied profound learning to the images

style._about: Counted per 1,000 words by stylometry.py; percentiles against human calibration text. Weak on their own: humans write like this too, and more so since 2023.

excess_vocabulary.about: Words whose frequency rose sharply in scientific writing after ChatGPT (Kobak et al. 2025 'style' words + Liang et al. 2024 peer-review adjectives).

tells.about: Phrasing patterns catalogued by Wikipedia's 'Signs of AI writing', blader/humanizer and stop-slop (MIT).
